verdict.reasoning: Patient presents with diarrhea as the main issue: 'it says here you have a... you're having problems going to the toilet.' Patient: 'like diarrhea... it's lasting for like three days.'
Patient says 'I just go into the toilet every 10 minutes' but this is about frequency of needing to go, not explicitly 'watery stools'; stool consistency is never described as watery.

Location and crampy quality: 'the pain is mainly focused in the center area of the abdomen, like under the belly button... sometimes I can hear my stomach, like the cramps.' Relief with bowel movement: 'it seems to be alleviate the toilet and maybe it's like gas.'
Patient confirms tenderness on palpation: Doctor: 'when you press on your tummy, does it cause any pain?' Patient: 'Oh, it does a little bit.'

One morning episode after fruit, no blood: 'I think it was this morning... I had some fruit... Then I got a bit of nausea and I vomited... I don't think there is blood because... it was strawberries that I was having for breakfast. So... it wasn't blood.'
Patient explicitly reports nausea before vomiting: 'Then I got a bit of nausea and I vomited.'
Patient denies blood in stool: 'Have you noticed any blood?' Patient: 'No, I haven't noticed any blood.' In context of diarrhea this refers to stool.
Patient denies chest pain: 'And how about chest? Have you noticed any chest pain?' Patient: 'No, I haven't. I haven't noticed any chest pain.'

Patient has baseline asthma but no new breathing issues: 'have you noticed any problems with your breathing?' Patient: 'I always have problems with my breathing because of the asthma... but a part of the normal. I haven't, I haven't.' This supports denial beyond baseline.
Fever denied with some sweating: 'I didn't have any fever recently. I was sweating a little bit last for bed, but I... don't think so.' This supports no fever and mild night sweats.

Decreased intake and uncertainty about fluids: 'I try not to eat a lot because I just go into the toilet every 10 minutes.' and 'Maybe I'm not drinking enough water... I think I don't drink enough water.'
Duration reiterated several times: 'it's lasting for like three days'; clinician: 'you've had the diarrhea for three days' and patient: 'Yes.'
Patient states asthma history: 'So I have... asthma and I take some inhaler.'

Patient uses an inhaler and recently changed brands: 'I take some... inhaler' and 'my inhaler kind of run out... I have this brand, but I bought a new one here. And I don't know, maybe this new one has caused it.' Brand name is not specified.

Patient says 'I have an allergy. I have nkda allergy.' This is ambiguous and does not clearly support 'no known drug allergies'; it suggests having 'an allergy' while also saying 'nkda', so documenting clean NKDA is not supported.
Family history: 'my father... died about 10 years ago of cancer.'
'Appears to live alone' is not mentioned; there is no discussion of living situation in the transcript.
Work impact is explicit: 'I can't go to work because I need to go like every... when I finish, I need to... I feel I need to go again.'
Alcohol and smoking use are not discussed anywhere; stating the patient denies them adds new information.
No vitals (BP, HR, temp, etc.) are mentioned anywhere in the transcript, so 'No vital signs are provided' is accurate.
Matches earlier tenderness: 'when you press on your tummy, does it cause any pain?' 'Oh, it does a little bit.'
Patient notes audible cramping/bowel activity: 'sometimes I can hear my stomach, like the cramps.' This supports patient-perceived active bowel sounds/cramping.
Beyond abdominal tenderness and patient-reported cramps, no other physical exam maneuvers or any labs/imaging are documented in the transcript.

Clinician assessment: 'what it sounds like to me is that you might have eaten something bad... This is normally called gastroenteritis, so an infection over the tummy.' Symptoms: three days diarrhea, abdominal pain, one episode of vomiting, no blood. Food-borne etiology is explicitly suggested.
Possible mild dehydration is not explicitly assessed; while patient may be at risk, the clinician never states dehydration or comments on it directly.
Asthma is mentioned but stability on inhaler is not formally assessed; clinician does not state 'asthma is stable' or similar.

Clinician advises fluids but does not mention oral rehydration solution: 'do three things. Number one is to drink lots of water and fluids because you're losing lots at the moment.' No advice about ORS is given.

Clinician advises looking out for fevers and seeing GP if getting much worse: 'make sure and look out for any fevers... if you feel you're getting much worse, then I would suggest you go and see your GP.' There is no explicit instruction to monitor for persistent vomiting, blood in stool, or worsening pain as discrete red flags.

'Three is stay home for the time being until you get slightly better.' plus patient already cannot go to work due to symptoms. This supports advice to rest at home and effectively avoid work until improved.
Clinician states antibiotics are not used: 'Normally things like antibiotics don't help. They make the situation worse.' No prescription is given, supporting no antibiotics at this stage.
While inhaler use and brand change are discussed, the clinician does not advise 'continue regular inhaler use' or 'seek a refill'; this is not part of the documented plan.

Safety-net: 'If you feel you're getting much worse, then I would suggest you go and see your GP in real life in person' and patient plans: 'I will wait a couple of days... and then I will book.' This covers advice to seek in-person review if deterioration or no improvement over ~24–48 hours.
